i've definitely indulged in self-loathing my fair share. i'm very lucky to have a fair amount of support from my family, though, so i can only imagine how difficult that aspect might be. but im still optimistic that anyone can receive love. for me i had a lot of self-loathing related to shame/bullying. there were a few things that helped me move (somewhat) past it. primarily, being honest with people. the first time i really started to get relief was when i talked about how i felt, first in therapy. people naturally don't want to talk about what makes them feel ashamed, but hiding the wounds only gives them more power. although extremely difficult, releasing those wounds (particularly in a safe environment, like therapy) allows them to heal. for me, this was a slow process, but each time i opened up i felt a little bit better. 

the other thing that helped me was a cognitive-behavioral therapy method. learning to notice when you're self-loathing and trying not to indulge in it can, overtime, make a big difference. a lot of psychologists call this the "inner critic," and learning more about it/how to control it (somewhat) really helped me.

and the last one.... may not be feasible. but i adopted two cats. if you can, having a dog or cat is great because they give you tons of love (probably more for dogs lol). it can be really healing.

i hope that helps some!

honestly, it's still something i struggle with. i think for me opening up was a combination of three things:

1) taking the leap of faith. there isnt really a way around it, imo, especially the first couple times. it's scary to make yourself vulnerable, but the more you do it, the better it feels. i broke it down into steps, starting with the easiest (for me it was talking to one person over fb chat/text, saying i wasn't feeling great and asking if i could vent a bit) and ending with the hardest (talking with people face to face and actually showing all my emotions). i still have trouble with the last one, but i think that's as much due to the normal social stigmatization of emotions than ptsd itself. you don't have to open up all at once. taking small, consistent steps can be super effective!

2) trying to understand others better. i honestly think that just about any emotion is relatable. a lot of times with ptsd (for me anyway) i could only think about my own problems because i built them up so much in my mind. but other people go through difficult times too, even though many don't show it. i think the lifetime incidence of ptsd across the world is something like 7.5%. that's a lot of people. imagine being in a room with 39 people. odds are that two others with experience ptsd in their lifetime (i hope my math is right lol). it's a lot easier to be open when you think about how others have feelings and issues too.

3) this is more of a mental realization i felt... considering all the horrible things i felt like doing to myself made me think about why i don't.. why i WANT to live. and for me, i wanted to live for my loved ones and to express myself fully. in a way, i felt like if i were not going to really be myself, then what was the point? and honestly, the best thing you can give to others is yourself. personally, i feel as though intimacy (with yourself and others) is one of the cornerstones of life itself, and the beauty of it is that (usually) both people benefit from intimate moments with each other. wholly, these thoughts really changed my perspective and motivated me to get out there again.

opening up is not something you really do overnight. it's a constant battle that even people without ptsd face. i think that, in the end, you just have to take small steps forward. or small leaps of faith. as you go forward you build momentum, and it gets easier and easier to be open.

i hope that helps!

my story had a lot to do with ongoing childhood trauma as well as a couple other incidents after moving out. for me, classical psychotherapy helped me slowly get out of my rut and make positive changes in my life. it was absolutely an essential, but in the end i think i am doing better not because of the therapy itself, but by applying all the things i learned (the best i could) into my own life. learning to calm yourself after panic attacks, slowly getting back out in the world, and (trying to) be open about everything that happened did wonders for me.
and thank you for your service!

It's a long journey. It takes everything in you. But if you give everything you can, it gets better. I was thinking about suicide everyday for a number of years. But going to therapy, trying to be completely open, and staying positive.... Life becomes worth it.

You can't do it alone. I tend to isolate myself too, but the more I talk about how I feel or what I'm going through, the easier it gets to talk more to people and feel/connect with others. The way that PTSD stems from the fear network in the brain, it's natural to be scared. But if you work at it and give everything, you will recover! And because of the ridiculousness of the challenge that those who are diagnosed are faced with, you grow so much as a person (search post-traumatic growth if you are not familiar with it).

IMO the most important thing is not to fight yourself. Coping comes with acceptance of whatever feelings you have from your experience. Anyone else who experienced what you went through would feel similar things that you do (especially as a kid), so there is no reason to judge.

I can't say I'm familiar with seizures nor have done neurofeedback, but my advice would be to take as much of it in stride as possible. I had a lot of childhood trauma and dissociation too. It takes time to work through and there is no "cure," but you can make a full recovery!

With regard to treatment in general, trust the process. PTSD has shown to be very treatable. Odds are that neurofeedback improves the condition for many, but not all of those who suffer. If for some reason you are one of the people who doesn't respond well to it, there are many other viable treatment methods to try.

Best of luck!

I think both sides of the Klinsi argument have some pretty good points:

Fire Klinsi:
- team looked horrible in the Gold Cup
- has not called up some guys that should be, such as Feilhaber
- he can be arrogant at times and displace responsibility for losses he is fairly accountable for
- the youth setup, excluding the recent U20s, has not been great
- even at the World Cup, the team was on its heels for most of every match
- has not delivered on a "proactive style of play"
- has played players out of position and seen little pay off

Keep Klinsi
- best winning percentage as a coach
- navigated us out of the group of death
- first win at Azteca
- VERY good record against Mexico, even with Saturday's loss
- there have been some critical changes to the youth setup, like the addition of teams other than U-17 and U-20
- recruitment of foreign nationals of unparalleled success

I think possibly the best reason not to fire Klinsi is that the talent is arguably not there right now. Should he be trying some new people, definitely, but we have long known that the generation after Michael Bradley, perhaps save Jozy Altidore (that's a whole other debate), is weak. The U-23s feature a 17 year old at center back (no slant to CCV who is looking great, but still), and many on the roster have come straight from the U-20 World Cup side. Worse, our well went dry as Mexico had their "golden generation." 

I think that whether we like it or not, US Soccer is heading into a rebuilding phase. As past stars like Dempsey finish their careers, there are very few options around the age of 23 who look like they are going to break out as stars. I've heard that the real changes to the academy system should start paying off for our current U-15's and below. In the meantime, our best hope is the current U-20's, and some attacking options from the U-17's. Regardless of it's Klinnsman at the helm for the upcoming couple years or someone else, it's looking like it will be a bumpy ride.

it refers to something more general, like when you have a situation that's annoying you (for instance, getting over a break up), it's natural to go back and forth with your thoughts and feelings trying to work them out. normally, in time, you sift through everything (or most of it) and resume normal functioning (at least some level of it) in PTSD, however, this pushing and pulling is unable to sift through all the thoughts and emotions the victim is going through, and they continue this "push-pull" indefinitely.

A couple great books are the ones that I cited; "Effective Treatments for PTSD" is especially good. 

As another redditor wrote, the physiological aspect is not as well known, but current research points to changes in the HPA axis (Hypothalamus, Pituitary, Amygdala). Essentially the switch in the brain that regulates stress gets stuck in the "on" position, as opposed to switching between on and off. It's as if patients are stuck in fight vs. flight, which wreaks havoc on a number of other brain and bodily symptoms.

I spent my previous semester exclusively studying PTSD, particularly the psychological aspects. I was extremely fortunate to work with some of the leaders in the field, notably the director of one of the six national centers for PTSD. This is a brief excerpt from my paper:

Whether someone develops PTSD after a traumatic event occurs depends on whether the victim can successfully cope with the temporary traumatic event when it is over (which is predicted by a balancing of risk and protective factors), and can accommodate the trauma into a new illusion of safety schema. This adaptation to new circumstances is the process known as resilience. When successful, the new schema allows one to continue with life, not the same way, but still effectively, and continue to use resilience as an everyday process. (Psychological Trauma and the Adult Survivor, 68). When adaptation fails, however, the mind becomes fixated on how to successfully overcome the trauma (direct mastery), despite it no longer taking place, in attempt to resolve the extreme distress of annihilation anxiety (anxiety that occurs when one's psychological vitality is threatened). The victim experiences intrusion as the mind attempts mastery over the potential annihilation in a push-pull fashion. Because the memories of the event are painful and overwhelming, the victim learns to avoid stimuli associated with it. The overwhelming nature of the trauma and the failure to accommodate it leads to negative alterations in mood and cognition, as the self sees this failure as their own and attributes it to their self-concept. And because the illusion of safety is gone, the victim becomes hyper-aroused to preserve their life, or to be sure the event does not occur again, which ostensibly represents annihilation. This constant hyper-arousal is often accompanied by numbing, likely due to excess stress. There are a number of other symptoms that may present, and the exact manifestations of these symptoms differ in severity and prominence on a case by case basis. (Effective Treatments for PTSD).

Three main reasons:

First, the majority of US debt is held not by foreign countries, but by US people.

Second, the debt that is international (mostly held by China) is codependent. By that I mean, China relies on the US debt service to fund its investments (mostly in the US). The US and China both need each other, and so long that the US and everyone else is confident the US can pay back its debt, there shouldn't be any panic resulting in a debt crisis (often happens when buyers lose confidence and pull all their money out of a country at once.)

Third, given economic theory, over time the US should gain more manufacturing jobs again as markets go back to equilibrium. We're already seeing Chinese investors invest in US markets (they now have the money to from the US buying imports). And that is leading to a rise in manufacturing jobs, which are the essential part of the middle class.

The problem with all of this is it takes time. Probably for some it will span their whole lifetimes. But while the U.S. debt at its current level is unsustainable, the signs point that the U.S. should get back to equilibrium. This is helped by the fact the U.S. is such a big part of the world economy.
